groups.title: A2A 101
groups.description: How one agent gives work to another agent that it cannot see inside. Each request, response, and stream event in this manual comes from a recorded run.

metadata.title: A2A 101
metadata.subtitle: The Agent2Agent protocol, from its purpose to each request and response
metadata.summary: How one agent gives work to another agent that it cannot see inside. Each request, response, and stream event in this manual comes from a recorded run.
metadata.audience: You are an engineer who has built an agent that calls tools or a model API. You know HTTP and JSON. You have not read the A2A specification.
outcomes: Read an agent card and say what the agent offers, how to reach it, and what it requires before you send anything.
Predict which state a task is in at any point of a run, and what a client is allowed to do next.
Choose between a blocking call, polling, streaming, and push notifications for a given job.
Read any A2A request, response, or stream frame line by line, in either JSON binding.
Name the errors a client must handle and the rules a server can break without noticing.

palette.meaning: the client agent and what it sends
remote agents, their cards, and the messages they send back
parts and artifacts: the content a task produces
tasks, task states, and transitions
the server's stored task records
streams, subscriptions, and push notifications
the model or logic inside an agent, which A2A never shows
tools and systems an agent calls on its own: CI, Git, MCP servers
errors, failure, rejection, and cancellation
the operator, the host, and anything outside the protocol

plate.title: One planner, three remote agents
plate.caption: The planner reads three cards and delegates three tasks: one completes at once, one after a question, and one after an operator approves. Lanes run top to bottom in the order of the planner log, and ids are shortened to 8 characters.

parts.title: The Protocol on One Page
parts.thesis: A2A standardizes how one agent finds another agent, gives it work, and follows that work, and it leaves the agent itself out of scope.

parts.title: AgentCard
parts.thesis: Before a client sends a message, the AgentCard tells it what the agent offers, where to reach it, and what it requires.

parts.title: Data Model
parts.thesis: Every A2A exchange is built from five objects: Message, Part, Artifact, Task, and the contextId that groups tasks.

parts.title: Operations
parts.thesis: Eleven operations create, read, cancel, and follow tasks, and each one has rules that a client must know before it calls.

parts.title: Bindings
parts.thesis: The same operations travel over JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON, and gRPC, with two headers and one error model shared by all three.

parts.title: Security and Extensions
parts.thesis: The card declares how to authenticate and which extensions apply, and the specification lists what each side must check.

parts.title: Implementing A2A
parts.thesis: A client and a server follow the rules of the earlier parts, and the official test kit checks the server against them.

reference.title: Reference
reference.thesis: Lookup tables for every name in the manual.
reference.summary: Operations by binding, objects and fields, task states, errors, a glossary, the sources, and the index of figures.

metadata.title: Docker Sandboxes and Docker Agent 101
metadata.subtitle: Isolated microVMs for coding agents, and the agent runtime that runs inside them, command by command
metadata.summary: How to run an agent you do not trust on files you do. Every listing in this manual comes from a recorded run of sbx and docker-agent on one Mac.
metadata.audience: You are an engineer who runs coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex on real repositories. You know Docker, git, and YAML. You have not used Docker Sandboxes or Docker Agent.
outcomes: Run a coding agent inside a sandbox, give it only the files it needs, and get its commits back without giving it your credentials.
Read one line of sbx policy log and say which rule allowed or blocked the connection, and what to change.
Write an agent file that runs a team of agents over local tools and a local model, record it, and replay it from a cassette.
Serve the same agent file over the HTTP API, MCP, ACP, and A2A, and share it as a signed OCI artifact.
Map any command from the 2025 Docker Sandboxes plugin or the cagent material to its current form.

parts.title: The Two Products on One Page
parts.thesis: sbx runs any agent inside a microVM it owns, docker-agent runs an agent file, and docker-agent run --sandbox joins them through a kit and the proxy.

parts.title: sbx policy, sbx secret, sbx mcp

metadata.title: Miles 101

metadata.summary: How to run GRPO with Miles on one GPU, choose a model that fits, and check that the run is correct. Every measured line comes from recorded runs on a DGX Spark.

plate.title: One GRPO step on one GB10
plate.caption: The SGLang engine and the FSDP trainer take turns on the Blackwell GPU. The one that waits stays parked in the same 128 GB pool. Medians of 48 steps on one GB10, from a run made before we added the heat guard.

metadata.audience: You can serve a model and you know what a reward is. You want to train a model with reinforcement learning, and you want to know which settings matter before you rent a cluster.
outcomes: Run GRPO on one GPU with the radixark/miles image and read the first ten steps.
Stop a run that keeps going after its rollout engine died.
Pick a model size that fits training and rollout on one GPU.
Check that a run is correct, and not only that it runs.
Find the cause of a failed run from its first symptom.

failure: a dead engine, an out-of-memory kill, a crash

metadata.title: Reverse Engineering 101
metadata.subtitle: Reading a compiled program you built, from file bytes to evidence-backed pseudocode, with rea and Ghidra
metadata.summary: How to read a compiled program without its source and prove what you found. Every listing comes from a recorded run of rea 6.7.0 and Ghidra 12.1.4 on programs written for this manual.
metadata.audience: You are an engineer who writes C, Python, or JavaScript and uses a coding agent. You have never read machine code with a decompiler. You want to understand what a compiled program does and to check what an agent tells you about it.
outcomes: Read the file header, sections, symbols, and relocations of a compiled program, and map an address to a file offset.
Run rea with the Ghidra provider on a program you built, and read its Evidence record: confidence, authority, limitations, and unknowns.
Find a function, read its assembly and pseudocode, follow its references, and say where the decompiler output is incomplete.
Prove a rebuilt function equal to the original by running both over an input grid and by comparing bytes after masking relocations.
Drive rea from an agent over MCP, and keep an evidence ledger that separates what was observed from what was inferred.

metadata.title: SGLang 101
metadata.subtitle: Serving language models with SGLang, from one request to a fleet, with the judgment the flag list leaves out
metadata.summary: How SGLang turns GPU memory and time into tokens, why each feature exists, and which defaults to trust. Local listings come from recorded runs of SGLang 0.5.22.
metadata.audience: You are an engineer who has called a model API and wants to serve an open model yourself. You know what a token and a GPU are. You have not read a serving engine's scheduler or cache, and you want to know which settings matter before you pay for them.
outcomes: Install SGLang, serve a model, and get the first answer from both of its APIs in about ten minutes.
Size the KV pool for your GPU, and fix a server that runs out of memory.
Tune the server for your traffic: shared prompts, long documents, many users, or FP8.
Benchmark your own server, and watch it in production with its metrics.
Choose how to scale to many GPUs, and judge a published benchmark before you trust it.

plate.title: One radix tree on one L4
plate.caption: On our L4, the system prompt is one shared node of the radix tree, and each repeat request attaches below it. The repeats had 2,998 of 2,999 tokens cached, and the first token came after 82.5 ms instead of 2,143.9 ms. From capture/gpu/out-l4/cache-experiment.txt and capture/gpu/out-l4/server-default.log.

parts.title: Start
parts.thesis: Install SGLang, serve a model, check that the server is healthy, and learn the two phases and four numbers behind every request.
parts.summary: Install with uv or Docker, the first answer from both APIs, the health checks and startup lines, then prefill against decode and the four numbers.

parts.title: The Request Path
parts.thesis: A request crosses three processes, and the scheduler between them decides who runs, who waits, and who gets thrown out.
parts.summary: sglang serve, the scheduler loop and its policies, admission and retraction, the overlap scheduler, and the response path.

parts.title: The KV Cache
parts.thesis: Memory, not compute, decides how many users one GPU can serve, and the radix tree decides how much of that memory you pay for twice.
parts.summary: Bytes per token, startup sizing, RadixCache, prefix-friendly prompts, eviction and HiCache, and hybrid models.

parts.title: Each Forward Pass
parts.thesis: Most decode time is launch overhead and memory traffic, so SGLang picks graphs, kernels, and draft tokens for your GPU before you ask.
parts.summary: ForwardMode and CUDA graphs, attention backends, quantization, speculative decoding, structured outputs, and deterministic inference.

parts.title: Measuring a Server
parts.thesis: A throughput number without a latency target describes nothing, so measure the knee before you tune anything.
parts.summary: sglang.benchmark.serving, the /metrics endpoint, and how to read benchmarks that other people publish.

parts.title: One Server Becomes a Fleet
parts.thesis: Split a model across GPUs only after one GPU is saturated, and split prefill from decode only after you measured that prefill hurts.
parts.summary: Tensor, data, attention-data, and expert parallelism, MoE serving, prefill-decode disaggregation, and the model gateway.

parts.title: Production and Training
parts.thesis: Operate SGLang with its defaults written down, and expect reinforcement learning to treat the server as part of the training loop.
parts.summary: Deploying and tuning in order, and SGLang as the rollout engine of Miles.

stages.title: Read a JSONL trace
stages.summary: Parse one JSON object per nonempty line. Require stable ids, names, finite start and end times, nonnegative token counts and an explicit ok or error state. A malformed line stops processing with its line number. Silently dropping bad spans would distort timing and cost conclusions. Times are relative milliseconds, not wall-clock timestamps.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript models spans while preserving runtime checks at the log boundary.

stages.title: Validate parent relationships
stages.summary: A child span must reference an existing parent and fit inside the parent interval. Check every ancestor chain for cycles and reject duplicate ids. Multiple roots are allowed because a trace can contain overlapping independent runs. Validation happens before aggregation so corrupted graphs cannot produce convincing charts.
stages.languageWhy: Maps provide stable identity lookup and sets expose cycles.

stages.title: Separate work time from waiting time
stages.summary: Inclusive duration is end minus start. Exclusive duration subtracts the union of immediate child intervals, not their sum, because parallel children overlap. Root interval union provides wall time across runs. Tokens are local per span and summed once. The slowest result names the span with greatest exclusive duration, avoiding a root that is mostly waiting on children.
stages.languageWhy: Interval arithmetic exposes concurrency without relying on a tracing library.

stages.title: Render an inspectable timeline
stages.summary: Generate a standalone HTML timeline with one row per span, scaled bars and error coloring. Escape span names before inserting them into markup. Include own time, total time, wall time, tokens and error count. Empty traces still produce a readable artifact. The output is a local static report and does not load third-party scripts.
stages.languageWhy: HTML can present the same typed analysis without a build pipeline or chart dependency.

It reports the format, the architecture, and the sections and segments with permissions and entropy. skills: Detect a binary format and parse its header
Map sections and segments with permissions and entropy
Read symbol tables and demangle C++ names
Follow imports, exports, relocations, and chained fixups
Recover function starts and score them against ground truth
Publish a JSON report, an HTML byte map, and a build diff
prerequisites: Python 3.10+ for the inspector and the grader
Phase 13 lessons 32, 40, and 41: ELF tables, linking and loading, and C++ names
Hexadecimal arithmetic, little-endian byte order, and the struct module
metadata.youWillBuild: A static inspector that reads ELF, PE/COFF, and Mach-O files you compiled and reports their layout, names, links, and function starts.
usefulFor: Check the contents of a build before a release: which sections are writable and executable, which libraries it imports, and which names strip removed.
Compare two builds of your own program and see which sections grew, which symbols moved, and which strings changed.

stages.title: Detect the format and parse the header
stages.summary: Read the magic bytes and identify ELF64, a COFF object, a PE32+ image, or Mach-O 64. Parse the file header of each into one shape: format, architecture, kind, entry point, and the raw fields. Read the Mach-O load commands in sequence. Refuse 32-bit, big-endian, universal, and truncated files with a FormatError that names the reason.
stages.languageWhy: struct.unpack_from with an explicit bounds check turns every header field into one checked read.

stages.title: Sections, segments, permissions, and entropy
stages.summary: List the sections of each format with name, address, file offset, size, and bytes in the file. Add an r/w/x permission string from the flags of the format. List ELF program headers and Mach-O segments. Compute Shannon entropy in bits per byte over the bytes each region holds in the file, so zero-fill regions report 0.
stages.languageWhy: collections.Counter and math.log2 give the entropy formula in three lines that you can check against a hand count.

stages.title: Symbols, string tables, and demangled names
stages.summary: Read ELF .symtab and .dynsym, COFF symbol records with their auxiliary entries, and Mach-O nlist_64 entries. Resolve each name through its string table with a bounds-checked C string read. Report value, size, kind, binding, and section. Demangle a documented subset of Itanium C++ names and return None for anything outside it.
stages.languageWhy: A small recursive-descent parser over a string shows the Itanium grammar and its substitution table without a library.

stages.title: Imports, exports, relocations, and chained fixups
stages.summary: Read ELF RELA records, COFF relocation records, Mach-O relocation_info, and PE base relocations. Read the PE import and export directories. Decode Mach-O chained fixups word by word into binds and rebases, and read the exports trie with ULEB128 values. Every pointer is checked before it is followed, and a chain or trie that loops or leaves its page fails.
stages.languageWhy: Integer shifts and masks decode packed 64-bit fixup words exactly as the loader does.

stages.title: Strings with sections and recovered function starts
stages.summary: Extract ASCII and UTF-16LE strings and name the section and segment that hold each one. Find function starts with five methods: symbols, LC_FUNCTION_STARTS, a prologue scan, direct call targets, and the entry point. Score each method against the symbol table of the unstripped build with precision and recall.
stages.languageWhy: Sets make true positives, false positives, and misses one operation each.

stages.title: JSON report, HTML byte map, and build diff
stages.summary: Compose every stage into one versioned JSON report and validate it. Render a standalone HTML report with a byte map. Each file slice takes its color from its region and its brightness from its entropy. Every string from the binary is escaped. Diff two reports to show section growth, moved and removed symbols, and changed imports, exports, and strings.
stages.languageWhy: json and html from the standard library produce a report that a script and a reviewer can both read.

stages.title: Turn DOM state into constrained actions
stages.summary: Read labels, values, disabled states and stable ids from a small form. Validate unique ids and field types. Choose one action at a time: fill the name, fill email, then click the uniquely identified Save request button. Page prose is never interpreted as instructions. Missing fields, ambiguous labels, dangerous buttons and unexpected origins cause an explicit blocked result.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript expresses observations and an action union with no arbitrary-script action.

stages.title: Stop on completion, stalling or budget
stages.summary: Observe after every action. Stop if the state repeats, if policy blocks an action, or if the step budget is consumed. Completion requires the DOM success flag and a separate screenshot check. Trace every selected action before execution. The fixture backend is explicitly a simulator; it supplies deterministic observations to test the loop and does not claim browser coverage.
stages.languageWhy: An injected driver separates the policy from Chromium and enables deterministic failure tests.

stages.title: Verify screenshot pixels in Python
stages.summary: Read the PNG signature, chunk lengths and CRCs, then decompress a bounded image payload. Reverse PNG row filters and count green success pixels. Combine this visual signal with the DOM flag; neither alone is sufficient. This is a narrow pixel-state detector for the authored fixture, not OCR or general vision. Corrupt, oversized, interlaced and unsupported color formats fail explicitly.
stages.languageWhy: Python stdlib can decode a bounded RGB/RGBA PNG without adding an imaging dependency.

stages.title: Drive the real fixture and score the run
stages.summary: Serve fixture.html over loopback and navigate to it with gstack browse. GstackDriver reads DOM observations, fills labels, clicks the observed button and captures a real screenshot. Commands use argument arrays instead of a shell. Run the same bounded policy with --live and compare its trace with the fixture backend. Keep completion scores separate for simulated and real-browser runs.
stages.languageWhy: Node child-process argv calls adapt the same driver contract to the installed gstack browser.

stages.title: Parse the untrusted boundary
stages.summary: A model response is a byte string. Parse the entire string as JSON, reject markdown wrappers and trailing text, and cap its UTF-8 byte size before parsing. Accept JSON primitives as well as objects: the schema, not the parser, determines whether a primitive is useful. Do not remove text until it happens to parse because that hides the actual output contract.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript keeps unknown data separate from typed application values.

stages.title: Walk a schema recursively
stages.summary: Implement object, array and primitive validation. Required properties are checked with own-property semantics. An inherited property does not satisfy the contract. Treat integer as a refinement of number, reject non-finite numbers, and preserve a path for every failure. Bound recursive descent at depth 32 so a schema and value cannot consume the stack indefinitely.
stages.languageWhy: Recursive union types describe the schema subset without importing a validator.

stages.title: Reject ambiguous and unsupported contracts
stages.summary: Add numeric bounds, enum membership, minimum Unicode string length, array bounds, and closed objects. Escape slash and tilde inside property paths. A keyword outside this educational subset is a configuration error, not silent success. This implementation intentionally does not claim complete JSON Schema conformance: references, formats and combinators require additional work.
stages.languageWhy: Typed issue objects make error reporting stable across the CLI and retry loop.

stages.title: Repair with a finite budget
stages.summary: Feed only structured validation feedback into a generation callback. Count each call before interpreting its output. Stop immediately after acceptance and return an explicit exhausted state after the final rejected attempt. Provider failures propagate instead of being disguised as schema failures. The trace records each attempt so a successful third response does not conceal two earlier contract violations.
stages.languageWhy: Async function types allow deterministic fake generation and a later provider adapter.

metadata.youWillBuild: A persistent memory workbench with revision history and one boundary for REST and MCP.

stages.title: Keep text, namespace and provenance together
stages.summary: Every memory needs a bounded id, namespace, text and source locator. Never return a detached string without its provenance. The small feature-hashing embedding maps normalized terms into a fixed vector; it is a deterministic lexical projection, not a pretrained semantic model. Hash collisions are expected and explain why lexical evidence remains part of retrieval.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript provides typed memory records; runtime validation protects JSON inputs.

stages.title: Serialize revisioned writes
stages.summary: Load a versioned event log and reconstruct the latest record for each namespace/id pair. An update must name its expected revision. Serialize writes so two callers racing from revision zero cannot both succeed. Append before mutating the in-memory map. This is a single-process store: append completion is not a power-loss durability guarantee, and multiple server processes require an external lock or database.
stages.languageWhy: Promises serialize local writes while JSONL makes the durable history inspectable.

stages.title: Score vectors in a real Rust process
stages.summary: Compile score.rs with the standard Rust toolchain and send query and document vectors over stdin. Compute cosine similarity, returning zero for a zero-norm vector. Combine 60 percent lexical query coverage with 40 percent cosine score and use ids to break ties. Test dimensions and finite values before crossing the process boundary. The Rust binary is compiled into a private temporary directory and removed on normal process exit.
stages.languageWhy: Rust handles the numerical kernel through a narrow line protocol; TypeScript owns retrieval and provenance.

stages.title: Expose REST and MCP tools
stages.summary: Bind a local server, require a bearer token, bound request bodies, and implement health, REST writes/search and the MCP initialization/tools subset over JSON-RPC POST. Tool execution failures use isError inside a successful JSON-RPC response; unknown protocol methods use a JSON-RPC error. This is a teaching subset without sessions, streaming or production authentication. Test actual HTTP bytes so serialization cannot drop source or revision.
stages.languageWhy: Node HTTP serves the same MemoryStore methods across two wire formats.

metadata.title: Mini Decompiler
metadata.tagline: A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset that turns functions in an object you compiled into structured C, then proves the output.
metadata.summary: A decompiler for a defined x86-64 subset that turns functions in an ELF relocatable object you compiled into structured C. It recompiles its own output, runs a differential test over an input grid, compares relocation-masked bytes and writes an evidence report that lists every unknown.
skills: Read ELF64 sections, symbols and RELA records
Decode an x86-64 subset and check it against a disassembler listing
Recover blocks, jump tables, dominators and loops
Lift to an IR with explicit flags and build minimal SSA
Fold copies, dead code and division by a constant
Recover System V parameters, pointer and struct types and signedness
Structure a graph into C without goto
Prove the output with recompilation, a differential grid and masked bytes
prerequisites: Python 3.10+ with the standard library only. clang is optional and enables the recompile and differential legs of stage 8.
Lessons on ELF anatomy, disassembly and control flow, lifting to pseudocode, calling conventions, compiler idioms and rebuild-and-prove.
metadata.youWillBuild: A decompiler that turns the functions of an x86-64 relocatable object you compiled into one C file, and an evidence report that says what was proved and what stays unknown.
usefulFor: Run python3 -m minidec verify on your own object and its source. The command writes decompiled.c, recompiled.o and report.json; a CI job can fail on status fail or unknown.

stages.title: Read an ELF relocatable object
stages.summary: Validate the ELF64 header, read section headers, the symbol table and every RELA record, and cut each function out of .text with its relocations and its alignment padding. A PC-relative record points at S + A + (end of instruction - P), so a target is resolved only with the end of the instruction that holds the field.
stages.languageWhy: struct.unpack_from reads fixed-layout tables with explicit little-endian formats and no third-party parser.

stages.title: Decode the x86-64 subset
stages.summary: Decode legacy prefixes, REX, one and two byte opcodes, ModRM, SIB, displacements and immediates for the instructions the fixtures use. Record where the displacement and immediate fields sit so relocations can be matched to operands. Every instruction must agree with the captured disassembler listing by address, bytes and AT&T text.
stages.languageWhy: Integer bit operations and dataclasses express each encoding field directly.

stages.title: Recover control flow
stages.summary: Follow control flow by recursive descent, resolve the position-independent jump table from its relocations and bounds check, split basic blocks, then compute dominators, dominance frontiers, post-dominators, back edges and natural loops. An indirect jump with no matching idiom stays unresolved and is reported.
stages.languageWhy: Dictionaries and sets carry the graph, and the iterative dominator algorithm needs no graph library.

stages.title: Lift to IR and build SSA
stages.summary: Lift each instruction to a small IR in which flags are an ordinary variable, frame bookkeeping disappears and frame-pointer slots become locals. Place phi statements on iterated dominance frontiers and rename over the dominator tree so every value has one definition, with explicit casts where a narrow definition meets a wide use.
stages.languageWhy: Frozen dataclasses give hashable IR expressions that can be compared and rewritten.

stages.title: Simplify and fold idioms
stages.summary: Turn flag conditions into comparisons, propagate copies and constants, delete dead definitions, merge congruent phis and substitute single-use values without moving a load across a store. Recognize the multiply-and-shift form of signed division by a constant and fold it only when the multiplier, shift and error bound prove the divisor.
stages.languageWhy: Python integers have no width, so 32 and 64-bit wraparound is explicit and testable.

stages.title: Recover the signature and types
stages.summary: A System V argument register read before any write is a parameter, and the highest one fixes the count. Coalesce phi webs into C variables, make a scaled element access a pointer to its element and constant offsets a struct, and choose signedness from the instructions that touch each value. Every choice carries its instruction evidence.
stages.languageWhy: Union-find over SSA keys and plain dictionaries keep each piece of type evidence inspectable.

stages.title: Structure the graph and emit C
stages.summary: Match loops, two-way and n-way conditionals with the immediate post-dominator as the join, emit if, if-else, while, do-while and switch, and print C with recovered struct and table definitions. A region that matches no shape produces a counted goto, and every heuristic goes into the unknowns list.
stages.languageWhy: String assembly with an explicit precedence table keeps the emitted C readable and compilable.

stages.title: Prove the output
stages.summary: Recompile the emitted C with the fixture flags, compare each function with relocation fields masked, compare the constants each relocation points at, and run original and candidate side by side over an input grid that crosses limits, zero, negatives and compare constants. The report is fail-closed and lists every unknown. Without clang the recompile and differential legs skip and say why.
stages.languageWhy: subprocess drives clang and the generated C driver, and json writes the evidence report.

prerequisites: Node22.18+ and Python3 for the grader
TypeScript objects, sets, promises, AbortSignal and precision/recall.
metadata.youWillBuild: A review disagreement workbench that measures when quorum helps and when it hides findings.
usefulFor: Input files maps names to text or lines. Optional reviewers contain id,cost,findings recordings. Expected labels use {file,line,rule}; the report records the source fingerprint and per-reviewer versus consensus metrics.

stages.title: Validate reviewer evidence
stages.summary: Require a file present in the supplied snapshot, a positive one-based line, an exact nonempty quote, a stable rule id and a severity from one through three. Evidence validation is shared across all reviewers. It protects the aggregation boundary against fabricated locations, but agreement and quoted text still do not prove a finding is correct.
stages.languageWhy: Unknown reviewer output must become a typed finding only after runtime validation.

stages.title: Aggregate independent support
stages.summary: Group valid findings by file, line and rule. Count one vote per reviewer per group, reject duplicate reviewer identities, and retain every severity vote. A quorum produces consensus; a singleton remains visible as needs-review. A disagreement flag survives consensus so the user can inspect conflicting severity judgments.
stages.languageWhy: Sets make reviewer identity and per-review deduplication explicit.

stages.title: Reserve costs and enforce deadlines
stages.summary: Reserve each reviewer cost before launching it. Skip work that cannot fit the remaining budget and record the decision. Race each reviewer against a deadline and abort its signal when time expires. Failures remain in the trace while completed reviews can still be aggregated. Adapters must honor AbortSignal to stop external work; the runner cannot force a remote service to cancel.
stages.languageWhy: Promises and AbortSignal allow parallel reviewer calls with explicit terminal states.

stages.title: Measure panel precision and recall
stages.summary: Evaluate unique finding ids against an expected set. Precision measures how many predicted findings are expected; recall measures how much of the expected set was found. Deduplicate both sets so repeated reviewers cannot inflate the metric. Zero predictions produce precision zero rather than a misleading perfect score. Try held-out inputs before adjusting quorum.
stages.languageWhy: Small pure metrics let deterministic fixtures establish a baseline before model integrations.

stages.title: Recover new-file line numbers
stages.summary: Parse hunk headers into old and new counters. Context consumes both counters, deletions consume only the old counter, and additions consume the new counter while producing a reviewable location. Reject truncated hunks and parent-traversing paths. The parser is deliberately for text unified diffs; binary patches and combined merge diffs are outside the contract. Wire Python into TypeScript using execFileSync and stdin, never an interpolated shell command.
stages.languageWhy: Python handles a streaming text grammar while TypeScript consumes a typed JSON boundary.

stages.title: Generate narrow review candidates
stages.summary: Build explicit static detectors for dynamic eval, shell exec, disabled TLS validation and empty catch handlers. Inspect only added lines. These patterns produce review candidates rather than proof of exploitable behavior. Keeping rule ids stable makes deduplication possible when a later model reviewer reports the same concern.
stages.languageWhy: Typed findings require a source quote, location and rule id before entering the report pipeline.

stages.title: Verify and merge findings
stages.summary: Require an existing added-line location and a nonempty exact source substring for every candidate. Reject fabricated files, deleted-line locations, empty quotes and invalid severity values. Merge findings by file, line and rule; keep the stronger severity when reviewers disagree. The quote gate establishes location support, not the truth of a security claim, which still needs review.
stages.languageWhy: A typed verification result keeps rejected model suggestions out of the renderer.

stages.title: Publish a local escaped report
stages.summary: Render a self-contained report with source locations, quoted evidence, severity and message. Escape source text as carefully as prose: a diff can contain executable HTML. Keep external publication outside the tool. The CLI writes review.html locally and prints a machine-readable summary for automation.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript joins verified data to HTML while escaping every untrusted string.

stages.title: Validate a portable bundle
stages.summary: Accept a named bundle with a SKILL.md and optional reference files. Validate every relative path before touching disk. Reject dot segments, absolute paths, drive prefixes, backslashes and reserved installation metadata. Limit each text file to 100 KB. The installer reads an in-memory bundle, leaving network fetching and signature trust as separate responsibilities.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript gives the bundle and agent destinations explicit contracts.

stages.title: Translate metadata and hash content
stages.summary: Keep one body of instructions while regenerating a small quoted metadata header. Preserve references byte-for-byte. Compute a SHA-256 digest over sorted path/content pairs, so file insertion order cannot change integrity. The digest detects changed content but does not establish publisher identity; obtaining a trusted expected digest is the caller's responsibility.
stages.languageWhy: Typed destination names constrain supported adapters to three known agents.

stages.title: Install atomically within a root
stages.summary: Check the expected digest before creating directories. Inspect each agent directory with lstat and reject symlinks. Stage the complete translated bundle beside the destination, then rename it. An existing managed installation moves to a temporary backup so a failed final rename can restore it. This educational transaction assumes a single trusted local writer; hostile concurrent filesystem replacement requires OS-level isolation.
stages.languageWhy: Node provides lstat, exclusive writes and directory rename for a bounded local transaction.

stages.title: Protect edits during upgrades
stages.summary: Before replacing an installation, verify that every tracked file still matches the prior digest and no unmanaged files have appeared. Refuse upgrades when users edited a tracked file or added their own file. The user can move those changes into the source bundle deliberately. Successful repeated installs leave no staging or backup directories behind.
stages.languageWhy: Digest comparison makes update behavior explicit instead of relying on timestamps.

metadata.youWillBuild: A routing debugger showing why the wrong skill activated and how to fix a rule.

SKILL.md provides standard name and description; routing.json is this project's documented local extension.

stages.title: Parse a typed skill catalog
stages.summary: A skill manifest declares an id, description, keywords, path patterns, priority, dependencies and permissions. Validate arrays and numbers at runtime rather than trusting a JSON cast. Tokenization normalizes punctuation and case and removes repeated words, so repeating a prompt cannot inflate its score.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript makes permission and dependency declarations visible before routing.

stages.title: Score words and repository paths
stages.summary: Award two points for each matched keyword and three for each matched file path. Return score reasons alongside the score. Support star within one path segment and double-star across segments, escape regular expression punctuation, and reject absolute or parent-traversing file paths. Resolve tied scores by priority and then id so ranking is reproducible.
stages.languageWhy: Small pure scoring functions are easy to inspect in a terminal and reuse in a web UI.

stages.title: Resolve dependencies before execution
stages.summary: Use depth-first traversal with separate active and visited sets. Active membership catches a cycle; visited membership avoids duplicate execution through a diamond. Validate permission requirements on dependencies as well as the selected skill. Emit dependencies before their consumers and reject unknown dependency ids instead of silently skipping work.
stages.languageWhy: A directed graph maps naturally onto typed arrays and sets.

stages.title: Abstain on ambiguous or blocked requests
stages.summary: Join ranking and dependency planning while preserving four distinct outcomes: ready, no-match, ambiguous and blocked. A score gap below the margin is ambiguous even if the tie-breaker produces a first result. A ranked winner can still be blocked by permissions. Return the ranked explanations in every outcome so a caller can display the decision.
stages.languageWhy: Discriminated status values prevent an uncertain route from becoming an execution request.

languageWhy.Python: Stdlib data structures, explicit algorithms and deterministic local tests.

stages.title: Decode the audio clock before processing
stages.summary: The integer samples 0, 16384 and -16384 become 0, 0.5 and -0.5. A sample index of 800 at 16000 Hz means 0.05 seconds. Interpreting the same index at 8000 Hz would double the timestamp without changing a single byte.
stages.languageWhy: Python standard-library collections, bytes and file operations expose this stage directly.

stages.title: Measure activity without claiming speech detection
stages.summary: At 1000 Hz, forty samples of amplitude0.5, twenty silent samples and forty active samples merge into [0,100] when gap_ms is40. The merged span lasts100 ms. A20 ms isolated burst is discarded when min_ms is40.
stages.languageWhy: Python standard-library collections, bytes and file operations expose this stage directly.

stages.title: Send real WAV bytes through a recognizer boundary
stages.summary: A provider timeout followed by success records attempts=2. Each output row retains start, end, text and the SHA256 of the exact encoded segment. A second segment cannot overlap the previous one, and fractional sample indices are invalid.
stages.languageWhy: Python standard-library collections, bytes and file operations expose this stage directly.

stages.title: Export a transcript you can hear and correct
stages.summary: The fixture CLI pairs the original spoken clip with its supplied reference text and labels the method clearly. Real recognition instead uses --endpoint. After inspecting playback, edit the rows in transcript.json and run --review-file to rerender; the report must match the original audio hash.
stages.languageWhy: Python standard-library collections, bytes and file operations expose this stage directly.

metadata.title: Self-Correcting Workflow Hooks
metadata.tagline: Turn repeated, sourced corrections into scoped rules, persist them atomically, and enforce only explicitly approved rules.
metadata.summary: Turn repeated, sourced corrections into scoped rules, persist them atomically, and enforce only explicitly approved rules.
skills: Capture corrections with provenance
Count independent sessions
Approve and select scoped rules
Persist rules across sessions
metadata.youWillBuild: A correction ledger showing why a rule exists, what it changed and how to undo it.
usefulFor: A correction ledger showing why a rule exists, what it changed and how to undo it.
capture, inspect, approve, retire and emit are file-based commands.

stages.title: Capture corrections with provenance
stages.summary: Preserve case-sensitive rule text and source excerpts with stable locators.
stages.languageWhy: TypeScript expresses the boundary between raw hook input and a validated correction.

stages.title: Count independent sessions
stages.summary: Group by scope and rule text with whitespace collapsed and case preserved. Deduplicate event ids and reject a reused id with different content. Count unique sessions rather than event count, so repeated hook delivery cannot promote a rule. Keep every source id attached to the candidate and sort the final output for reproducible files.
stages.languageWhy: Maps and sets let you separate repeated events from independent supporting evidence.

stages.title: Approve and select scoped rules
stages.summary: Require independent-session support before an explicit approval transition. Retired rules cannot be silently resurrected. At hook time, include only approved rules matching the current scope or global scope. Return source ids with injected rule text so the user can trace where persistent guidance came from.
stages.languageWhy: A state union makes candidate, approved and retired behavior explicit.

stages.title: Persist rules across sessions
stages.summary: Write a versioned JSON snapshot to a unique sibling temporary file with owner-only permissions, then rename it into place. Readers see the old or new complete file. Missing storage means an empty collection, while malformed storage is an error. This snapshot store supports one writer process; cross-process merge and locking are a separate extension.
stages.languageWhy: Node filesystem APIs support atomic replacement without another dependency.

entries.title: Label Adjudication Desk

entries.title: Lost Item Match Desk

entries.title: Presentation Rehearsal Coach
entries.summary: Help a speaker improve a rehearsal by aligning supplied slide text and timed transcript segments. Compute explicit pacing and topic-coverage signals, show the source phrases behind suggested practice targets, and export a slide-by-slide HTML report with a reusable rehearsal comparison file.

entries.title: Semantic Cache Correctness Lab
entries.summary: Build an opt-in answer cache that binds entries to tenant, model, source revision and expiry. Compare exact and semantic candidate matching using authored near-miss questions, including changed numbers and negation. Export a local HTTP adapter and a false-hit report; similarity alone must not authorize cross-user reuse.

entries.title: Tool Contract Migration Checker
entries.summary: Help tool authors evolve a callable interface while existing agents still hold old argument shapes. Compare a documented subset of before-and-after schemas, generate counterexamples for required fields and narrowed values, and replay saved calls through both validators. Export a compatibility report and reviewable migration fixtures for CI.

entries.title: Video Highlight Storyboard
entries.summary: Help a tutorial creator assemble short excerpts from a supplied video, frame samples and timed transcript. Combine visible shot changes with transcript topic scores, preserve exact source time ranges, and export a playable storyboard and edit-decision JSON for a video editor.

entries.title: A2A Task Handoff Workbench
entries.summary: Help teams connect agents that expose different capabilities and task lifecycles. Read Agent Cards, choose a mutually supported binding, and run a handoff that includes a request for more input, cancellation and a final artifact. Export a local client-server pair and a replayable receipt showing every state transition and artifact owner.

entries.title: Abstention Calibration Workbench
entries.summary: Help teams set a defensible accept-or-defer rule for a bounded task. Tune a score threshold on labeled development records under explicit error costs, freeze that policy, and evaluate held-out risk and coverage across slices. Export a decision-policy file and audit that shows how many requests need human review.

entries.title: Artifact Provenance Gate
entries.summary: Help a maintainer inspect a downloaded agent plugin or release artifact before integrating it. Verify the subject digest and attestation signature, evaluate declared builder and source identities against an explicit policy, and preserve the reason for every rejection. Export a CI gate with authored signed fixtures and a separately verified external-verifier adapter.

entries.title: Context Compaction Verifier
entries.summary: Help agent developers avoid losing a user constraint during a long session. Track explicit facts and constraints with source locators, create an extractive compressed context, and test candidate summaries against a declared retention contract. Export compaction middleware that keeps the prior snapshot when required evidence disappears.

entries.title: Local Inference Capacity Planner
entries.summary: Help a team choose a concurrency limit for its own model endpoint. Replay an authored arrival schedule, record queue wait separately from service time, and compare observed percentiles and timeouts across bounded runs. Export a capacity curve and editable operating limit based on measured requests, not model-name lookup tables.

entries.title: MCP Compatibility Doctor
entries.summary: Help an integration author diagnose a client that connects but cannot use a server correctly. Run authored negotiation, request-correlation and capability probes through a bounded transport adapter. Export a compatibility matrix and the smallest wire transcript that explains a failure, with credentials removed.

entries.title: Metamorphic Evaluation Workbench
entries.summary: Help evaluators catch inconsistent behavior across related inputs. Author transformations such as unit conversion, record reordering and equivalent formatting, define the output relationship each should preserve, and shrink violating examples. Export a property-based evaluation runner and small failure bundles that can be consumed by CI.

entries.title: OAuth Resource Boundary Lab
entries.summary: Help developers integrate delegated authorization without accepting a token intended for another service. Build local authorization and resource fixtures, follow metadata discovery, bind authorization to the requested resource, and check audience and scope at the server. Export reusable validation middleware and a redacted explanation of rejected requests.

entries.title: Outbound Request Policy Proxy
entries.summary: Help developers constrain a fetch tool that follows URLs supplied by untrusted documents. Evaluate the scheme, host, resolved address and each redirect, then connect using the validated destination under explicit size and time limits. Export a local egress adapter and loopback cases that reveal redirect and address-policy mistakes.

entries.title: Release Canary Decision Lab
entries.summary: Help a team decide whether an agent behavior change is ready for wider exposure. Assign stable request cohorts, compare candidate and baseline error and latency windows, and distinguish insufficient evidence from a failed gate. Export replayable decision receipts and a local shadow adapter that exercises the policy without deploying anything.

entries.title: Secret Injection Sidecar
entries.summary: Help developers keep service credentials out of model-visible tool arguments and routine traces. Build a local broker that resolves opaque handles, binds each handle to a destination and operation, and inserts environment-supplied credentials at the network boundary. Test echoed credential markers and export decision receipts with bounded response filtering.

entries.title: Tenant Fairness Scheduler
entries.summary: Help platform developers share a finite worker pool across tenants with different job sizes. Implement weighted deficit scheduling, bounded admission and aging, then compare per-tenant wait distributions under authored bursts. Export a queue adapter and workload receipts that make starvation and unused capacity visible.

entries.title: Agent Resource Deadlock Lab
entries.summary: Help developers coordinate agents that need several exclusive resources, such as a browser session and a workspace. Build wait-for graphs, explore bounded schedules, and compare ordered acquisition with timeout-and-release policies. Export deadlock traces and a resource-coordinator adapter with explicit acquisition receipts.

entries.title: Judge Bias Calibration Lab
entries.summary: Help evaluators decide whether an automated pairwise judge is useful for their task. Blind candidate identities, swap answer positions, run authored length counterfactuals and compare decisions with held-out human anchors. Export disagreement and bias breakdowns plus a versioned rubric and judge configuration receipt.

entries.title: Trajectory Counterexample Minimizer
entries.summary: Help agent developers diagnose failures that depend on action order. Express bounded temporal rules such as approval preceding an effect, check event traces, and remove irrelevant events while preserving declared causal dependencies. Export a minimal replay bundle with the violated rule and exact event identities.

entries.title: Transactional Workspace Patch Broker
entries.summary: Help concurrent coding agents avoid overwriting each other's files halfway through a multi-file change. Bind a patch bundle to content hashes, apply it to a private versioned workspace, run declared checks, and publish by switching one workspace pointer. Export a transaction API with conflict evidence and an explicit rollback journal.

entries.title: Agent Skills Engineering
entries.summary: Build, route, secure, evaluate, package, and verify Agent Skills in real hosts.

metadata.title: Agent Skills Engineering
metadata.summary: Build, route, secure, evaluate, package, and verify Agent Skills in real hosts.

prerequisites.title: Files, Python, and the command line
prerequisites.description: You can edit a text file, inspect a directory, and run a Python command. No agent framework experience is required.

prerequisites.title: Node.js, npx, and Python 3 for real labs
prerequisites.description: The install and bundled-script checkpoints require working node, npx, and python3 commands. The website and docs remain a conceptual fallback when these commands are unavailable.

prerequisites.title: One selected skill-capable host and install scope
prerequisites.description: Choose a supported agent host plus a writable project or user skill scope before installation. Record the exact host, scope, and installed path; do not infer discovery from installer success.

prerequisites.title: The Tool Interface
prerequisites.description: Skim this first if tool schemas and side-effect boundaries are new to you.

prerequisites.title: Tool Schema Design
prerequisites.description: Skim this first if you have not designed typed tool contracts.

prerequisites.title: Tool poisoning and untrusted instructions
prerequisites.description: Before Lesson 26, explain why skill and tool metadata is untrusted input. Lesson 15 is an optional refresher outside this five-lesson route when this preflight is not yet confirmed.

invocation.portableFallback: Use learn-agent-skills to start or resume the Agent Skills Engineering path.

metadata.conceptualFallback: Read the website or each lesson's docs/en.md manually. Mark real-host discovery, invocation, script, update, and uninstall evidence pending until Node.js, npx, Python 3, a compatible host, and a writable install scope are available.

quickStart.goal: Create a small skill, install the complete reviewer bundle into a real host, invoke it explicitly, verify its output, and remove it cleanly.
quickStart.workingDirectory: An empty learner workspace. Save its absolute path as TARGET_ROOT before installation.
expectedEvidence: The installer reports the selected host and destination.
The host discovers skill-contract-reviewer after a rescan or new session.
An explicit invocation returns a validation report and primitive choice, plus the resolved script path, target path, cwd, argv, and exit code.
The uninstall command removes only skill-contract-reviewer from the selected host.

lessons.title: Agent Skills: Portable Contract and Runtime Boundary
lessons.checkpoint: Create, install, invoke, verify, and remove one complete skill bundle in a real host.

lessons.title: Skill Discovery and Progressive Disclosure
lessons.checkpoint: Trace discovery, catalog publication, activation, and branch-specific resource loading separately.

lessons.title: Skill Invocation and Routing
lessons.checkpoint: Exercise explicit invocation, implicit selection, abstention, and a near-miss request.

lessons.title: Skill Permissions, Sandboxes, and Trust
lessons.checkpoint: Distinguish instructions, permission prompts, sandbox containment, and independent verification with observed evidence.

lessons.title: Skill Evals, Packaging, and Portability
lessons.checkpoint: Run the release gate in a real host, record routing and authority evidence, and verify upgrade and uninstall behavior.

optionalLessons.title: Capstone: Stateless Tool Ecosystem
optionalLessons.entryRule: Complete the Agent Skills route and Phase 13 lessons 06 through 20 before starting this systems integration capstone.

metadata.title: Agent Systems Engineering
metadata.summary: Engineer tool-using agent loops with explicit context, memory, orchestration, safety, evaluation, and production control.
metadata.keywords: agentic ai engineer agents tools mcp memory orchestration safety evaluation runtime observability
metadata.decisionPrompt: Do you want to engineer tool-using systems whose state, decisions, failures, and controls remain observable?
metadata.mission: Build on shared foundations to create agent systems with explicit tool contracts, state, safety boundaries, evaluation, and runtime evidence.
responsibilities: Design tool contracts and close the thought, action, observation loop.
Control context, memory, state transitions, and orchestration.
Model failures and defend tool and instruction boundaries.
Evaluate behavior and operate the runtime from traces and controls.
goodFitIf: You enjoy reasoning about stateful systems, control flow, and failure recovery.
You want autonomy to be bounded by explicit contracts and evidence.
You prefer testable orchestration over opaque agent demos.
baseline: Complete the shared software engineering and AI foundations, or demonstrate equivalent working knowledge.
Be able to build an API-backed LLM application and read structured traces.
Understand basic testing, state management, and security boundaries.
metadata.boundary: This is a specialist overlay after shared foundations. MCP is one integration surface, not the definition of agent systems engineering, and the route does not replace distributed systems or live operations experience.
metadata.timeNote: The estimate covers lesson time only. Portfolio work and practice take additional time.

portfolioProof.description: Turn a documented workflow into a narrow pilot with explicit evidence, release controls, and a feedback plan.
evidence: Workflow evidence and an assumption map
An executable specification for the smallest testable slice
A working vertical slice with evaluation results
Success metrics and a staged rollout plan
A feedback record that drives the next decision

readinessCriteria: Can separate the requested output from the underlying operational outcome.
Can rank assumptions by uncertainty and consequence.
Can build a vertical slice that tests one valuable workflow end to end.
Can define evaluation, success, rollback, and feedback criteria before release.
Can explain what evidence supports moving from prototype to pilot or production.
metadata.completionClaim: Completing this route shows that you can produce evidence for a scoped customer AI pilot. It does not guarantee a role or establish production experience.

metadata.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
metadata.summary: Build, secure, verify, and operate stateless MCP systems from JSON-RPC envelopes through conformance release gates.

prerequisites.title: Python and command-line basics
prerequisites.description: You can inspect JSON, edit a file, and run a Python command. Prior MCP or agent-framework experience is not required.

prerequisites.title: Python 3 for executable wire evidence
prerequisites.description: The deterministic implementations and tests use Python 3. A TypeScript runner is optional for the second Lesson 07 implementation.

prerequisites.title: The Tool Interface
prerequisites.description: Skim this lesson if typed tool calls and side-effect boundaries are new to you.

prerequisites.title: Tool Schema Design
prerequisites.description: Skim this lesson if you have not designed or validated JSON Schema tool inputs.

invocation.portableFallback: Use learn-mcp to start or resume the Model Context Protocol (MCP) path.

metadata.conceptualFallback: Read the website or each lesson's docs/en.md and hand-trace the named request and response pair. Record the checkpoint as conceptual and leave runtime, transport, authorization, and deployment evidence pending until the repository and Python 3 are available.

quickStart.goal: Run one stateless MCP transcript and identify the metadata that makes every request independently interpretable.
expectedEvidence: Each request repeats protocol version and client capabilities in params._meta.
server/discover returns a complete result with supported versions, capabilities, cache hints, and server identity.
An unsupported version returns JSON-RPC error -32022 with requested and supported versions.
The transcript closes its transport without creating or terminating an MCP protocol session.

publicDeploymentGate.appliesBefore: Any non-loopback bind, shared ingress, hosted endpoint, registry publication, or other public MCP deployment.
requiredEvidence: The Lesson 15 executable checkpoint rejects poisoned or drifted metadata before routing.
Tool descriptions, annotations, server instructions, and MRTR content are treated as untrusted input.
Authentication, authorization, sandboxing, and result verification are recorded as separate controls.
The learner explicitly approves the external deployment action after reviewing the target and authority.

lessons.title: MCP Fundamentals: Stateless Requests and JSON-RPC
checkpointEvidence: A transcript of two independent requests that each carry protocol version and client capabilities in params._meta.
A complete server/discover result and an unsupported-version error with code -32022.

lessons.title: Building an MCP Server: Stateless Python and TypeScript
checkpointEvidence: A server demo showing discovery, tools/list, and tools/call without connection-scoped protocol state.
A deterministic test result from the Python implementation, plus the TypeScript demo when a TypeScript runner is available.

lessons.title: Building an MCP Client: Discovery, Routing, and Dual-Era Fallback
checkpointEvidence: A client transcript that selects the modern route from per-request metadata and records the selected protocol era.
A separate legacy fallback trace that does not mix initialization state into the modern request path.

lessons.title: MCP Transports: stdio and Stateless Streamable HTTP
checkpointEvidence: A byte-framed stdio exchange and a POST /mcp exchange with the observed status and content type.
A header-to-body parity failure that is rejected before version negotiation or dispatch.

lessons.title: MCP Resources and Prompts: Addressable Context for Stateless Servers
checkpointEvidence: A transcript that lists and reads a URI-addressed resource and renders a prompt with validated arguments.
Explicit cache scope, TTL, deterministic ordering, and primitive choice for the same example.

lessons.title: MCP Model Input: Sampling Migration and Stateless MRTR
checkpointEvidence: An MRTR input request, a client-side provider result, and a retry of the original operation with a new request id.
Evidence that the server never emits an independent server-initiated JSON-RPC request.

lessons.title: Explicit Scope and Stateless Elicitation
checkpointEvidence: A request whose allowed roots are explicit operation inputs rather than remembered client state.
An elicitation MRTR response that is schema-validated before the original operation is retried.

lessons.title: MCP Tasks Extension: Durable Work on a Stateless Core
checkpointEvidence: A durable task trace covering creation, status polling, cancellation, and a terminal result across independent requests.
Task ids, revision or idempotency behavior, deterministic listings, and request-header parity recorded separately from protocol state.

lessons.title: MCP Apps on the Stateless Protocol
checkpointEvidence: A tool result that references an explicit UI resource and keeps protocol data separate from view state.
A recorded host-to-view message boundary with allowed messages, rejected messages, and no ambient authority assumption.

lessons.title: MCP Security: Poisoned Metadata, Routing, and MRTR State
checkpointEvidence: A poisoned or drifted descriptor rejected before tool routing and authorization.
A threat-model record that separates untrusted metadata, requested authority, sandbox boundary, and result verification.

lessons.title: MCP Authorization: CIMD, Issuer Binding, PKCE, and Step-Up
checkpointEvidence: A complete authorization trace with issuer-bound metadata discovery, PKCE, resource binding, audience validation, and least-privilege scopes.
A step-up decision that denies insufficient authority before the handler runs.

lessons.title: MCP Auth in Production: Issuer-Bound Enrollment and Tokens
checkpointEvidence: An issuer-bound client enrollment and token-validation trace with no discovery metadata trusted across issuers.
Independent authentication and concrete-operation authorization evidence for two consecutive requests.

lessons.title: Stateless MCP Gateways and Registry Admission
checkpointEvidence: A registry candidate admitted or rejected from immutable descriptor, provenance, and policy evidence.
A gateway trace that records deterministic routing, request-scoped authorization, and the exact policy snapshot used.

lessons.title: MCP Tool Contracts and Content
checkpointEvidence: A tool descriptor accepted only after schema, annotations, transport-header mappings, and content-block invariants agree.
A redacted HTTP-boundary trace that proves parameter-header encoding and exact header-to-body comparison before dispatch.

lessons.title: MCP Reliability, Cancellation, and Flow Control
checkpointEvidence: Four deterministic cancellation, completion, deadline, and disconnect orderings with no sleep-based coordination.
Exactly one terminal outcome per request, bounded queue behavior, and late-event handling recorded for every race.

lessons.title: MCP Registry Supply Chain: Admission, Drift, and Rollback
checkpointEvidence: A namespace collision and descriptor-drift case rejected before registry exposure.
A status transition and rollback decision tied to immutable artifact identity, provenance, and policy evidence.

lessons.title: MCP Conformance Engineering: Versioning, Evidence, and Operations
checkpointEvidence: A conformance matrix that records protocol era, additive-field behavior, SDK transformation, and proxy preservation at every boundary.
A release decision backed by normalized wire transcripts, deterministic tests, and an explicit failure report for every rejected case.

optionalLessons.title: Capstone: Stateless Tool Ecosystem
optionalLessons.entryRule: Complete the 17 required Model Context Protocol (MCP) lessons plus both prerequisite paths before starting this integration capstone.

entries.title: Reverse Engineering
entries.summary: Read a compiled program you built yourself: parse the file, decode the instructions, lift them to pseudocode, record evidence, and prove a rebuild equal, then learn the field around that pipeline with its main tools.

metadata.title: Reverse Engineering
metadata.summary: Read a compiled program you built yourself: parse the file, decode the instructions, lift them to pseudocode, record evidence, and prove a rebuild equal, then learn the field around that pipeline with its main tools.

prerequisites.title: Python, hexadecimal, and the command line
prerequisites.description: You can read Python, run a command, and convert between hexadecimal and decimal. No prior assembly or binary analysis experience is required.

prerequisites.title: Python 3.10 or later
prerequisites.description: Every reader, decoder, lifter, and ledger in the path uses the Python standard library only. The compiled fixtures are in the repository.

prerequisites.title: clang for rebuilding fixtures and Lesson 36
prerequisites.description: clang rebuilds the fixtures from source and compiles the Lesson 36 differential driver. Without it, Lesson 36 reads the committed objects and reports its behaviour claims as unknown.

prerequisites.title: Analyze only programs you built or are authorized to analyze
prerequisites.description: Before Lesson 32's lab, confirm that every target is a program you wrote and compiled, or one with written authorization. Lesson 32 opens with the law and the authorization rules.

invocation.portableFallback: Use learn-reverse-engineering to start or resume the Reverse Engineering path.

metadata.conceptualFallback: Read the website or each lesson's docs/en.md and trace the named fixture by hand. Record the checkpoint as conceptual and leave decoder, lifter, ledger, and proof evidence pending until the repository and Python 3 are available.

quickStart.goal: Parse one compiled object you did not hand-write the bytes of, and name its sections, symbols, and relocations.
expectedEvidence: The reader names the file format from its first four bytes.
The section table, the four function symbols, and the relocation records print with their offsets.

lessons.title: Program Anatomy: An ELF Reader From Scratch
lessons.checkpoint: Parse an ELF64 and a Mach-O fixture, and match the section, symbol, and relocation output against the recorded reference.

lessons.title: Disassembly and Control Flow: From Bytes to a Graph You Can Check
lessons.checkpoint: Decode the fixture functions with a result that matches llvm-objdump, then build the control-flow graph and its dominators for grade.

lessons.title: Lifting to Pseudocode: IR, SSA, and Structuring From Scratch
lessons.checkpoint: Lift percent_change to SSA and structured pseudocode, and explain each difference from the Ghidra output.

lessons.title: Evidence, Confidence, and Unknowns in Binary Analysis
lessons.checkpoint: Record one finding as an evidence entry with its confidence, limitations, and residual unknowns, and recompute its evidence id.

lessons.title: Rebuild and Prove Equal: Differential Tests, Byte Comparison, and the Evidence Loop
lessons.checkpoint: Run the differential grid and the relocation-masked byte comparison on a rebuilt function, and record the result as evidence.

lessons.title: The Reverse Engineering Landscape: History, Tool Families, and How a Decompiler Is Built
lessons.checkpoint: Run the comparison harness on the four fixture functions and explain each place where a tool invents or misses code, then name the same pipeline stage in three tools.

lessons.title: Calling Conventions and Stack Frames: System V, Windows x64, and AArch64
lessons.checkpoint: Infer parameter count, frame size, and saved registers for one function under three ABIs, and cite the spec rule behind each inference.

lessons.title: Compiler Idioms: What Optimization Does to Your Code and How to Read It Back
lessons.checkpoint: Recover a divisor from its magic multiplier and shift, and classify the switch lowering of one function at -O0 and -O2 with the evidence instructions.

lessons.title: Linking, Loading, and Stripped Binaries: PLT, GOT, Imports, Fixups, and Function Identification
lessons.checkpoint: Trace one imported call through its stub and fixup in a Mach-O build, and name the functions of a stripped build with signatures made from the unstripped one.

lessons.title: Recovering Data and Types: Structs, Arrays, C++ Objects, and DWARF
lessons.checkpoint: Infer a struct layout from memory accesses and match every field against the DWARF reader, then resolve one virtual call to its vtable slot.

lessons.title: Dynamic Analysis of Your Own Program: Debuggers, Traces, and Confirming Static Claims
lessons.checkpoint: Grade the static claims for one build as confirmed, refuted, or not observed from a debugger transcript, and explain the -O2 build where breakpoints never hit.

lessons.title: Beyond Native Code: Python, JVM, .NET, and WebAssembly Bytecode
lessons.checkpoint: Parse the same function from a .pyc, a class file, and a Wasm module, match each listing against the reference tool, and list what each container keeps.

lessons.title: Binary Diffing and Symbolic Execution: Matching Functions and Solving for Inputs
lessons.checkpoint: Match functions between two optimization levels with the staged matcher, show the relocation case that masking fixes, and solve one input for each path of grade.

lessons.title: AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering: LLM Decompilers, Analysis Agents, and Ground Truth
lessons.checkpoint: Score the candidate reconstructions on all six scorecard fields and explain the failing evidence for each candidate that does not pass.
